headline: High-risk shared filesystem and overlapping write/network capabilities make Cursor+ECC dangerous by default for prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor ingests workspace files, open buffers, and clipboard contents, while ECC uses files and skills as a primary workflow surface. Because both can read/write the same local filesystem and Cursor supports MCP, attacker-controlled content can cross from one agent into the other without provenance checks. This is a real interaction path, not a hypothetical one.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or ~/.claude-related files
IF one agent writes instructions into files the other later reads as trusted context
mitigations: Separate workspaces and config roots for each agent
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents
Require provenance tags on files before either agent reads them
Turn off MCP for one side during cross-agent work
requires-engineering: add a trusted/untrusted content boundary in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents; ECC touches session summaries, skills, hooks, MCP configs, and git history. Both have filesystem read/write and network egress, so sensitive material can move from shared local files into either agent’s outbound requests. The shared filesystem path makes leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF the same machine stores code, session files, or secrets for both agents
IF either agent is allowed to upload file contents to its backend or external APIs
mitigations: Store each agent in a separate OS account or home directory
Exclude secrets and session files from both agents’ workspaces
Disable automatic file-context upload for sensitive directories
Review and prune shared clipboard use before switching agents
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. Cursor explicitly supports shared state via local filesystem, and ECC warns that Cursor and Claude Code need separate roots to avoid overwriting session files. That is a direct write-conflict pathway with potentially destructive repo or config corruption.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or config directory
IF either agent runs with auto-apply or Yolo-style execution enabled
mitigations: Use separate git worktrees or clones
Assign distinct config roots for each agent
Disable auto-apply on at least one agent
Pause one agent while the other performs writes
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared mutable paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s workflow surface centers on skills, hooks, and agent delegation, so it can treat upstream outputs as actionable inputs. Cursor can generate code, shell commands, and file edits that ECC may then reuse. Without a verification gate, one agent’s mistaken output can cascade into the other’s downstream actions, including commits or external API calls.
conditions: IF ECC consumes Cursor-produced files, commands, or notes as authoritative
IF either agent is allowed to execute or commit based on the other’s output without review
mitigations: Insert a human review step before commits or API calls
Require explicit verification of generated facts and commands
Keep one agent read-only when the other is producing artifacts
Log and diff all handoffs between agents
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent outputs

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is a closed-source desktop editor with broad network egress and BYOK/API-key handling, while ECC is source-available and stores session summaries, hooks, and agent data under local paths. The pair creates a compliance mismatch around retention and data handling, especially if regulated code or secrets are placed into shared local files or external APIs.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in shared workspace files or session summaries
IF external APIs receive content that one agent retains longer than the other
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared agent workspaces
Document retention settings for both tools
Disable API-backed features for sensitive projects
Review which files each agent persists locally
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion policies across both systems
